title: Athens
html_source:
While making fun of their Greek-influenced names he suggest a trip to Athens: the largest city and capital of Greece both Ancient and modern.

For Stephen and for Joyce, the significance of going or not going to Athens reflects the fact that Joyce, although a polyglot and in general a virtuoisic linguist, never really learned Ancient Greek. (Slightly later in this chapter, Mulligan tells Stephen that he should learn the language, and that maybe Mulligan should be the one to teach him.) This is also perhaps an oblique comment on the fact that Ulysses is a modern update of the Odyssey, and also of the fact that Joyce’s immersion in Homer could be seen, at certain stages, as not particularly deep. Joyce’s original fascination with Ulysses (Odysseus) and the Odyssey was bound up not with the original text but with Charles Lamb’s retellings of it in The Adventures of Ulysses—themselves a modern update on the original Homeric poem.
